questions.question: A file named `calc.hs` contains `module Calculator where`. What happens when another file does `import Calculator`?
options: It succeeds, because module content matters, not the filename
GHC reports 'Could not find module Calculator', because it searches for Calculator.hs
GHC automatically renames calc.hs to Calculator.hs
It succeeds only if calc.hs is loaded first in the same GHCi session
questions.explanation: GHC finds a module by searching for a file with the matching name — Calculator.hs, not calc.hs. Even though calc.hs genuinely contains module Calculator, the search fails before GHC ever reads the file's contents.
optionFeedback: The convention is enforced exactly when a module is imported by name, because that is when GHC must search the filesystem for a matching file.
Correct — GHC's module search is filename-based. It looks for Calculator.hs and does not find it, regardless of what calc.hs contains.
GHC never renames files on your behalf; you must rename calc.hs to Calculator.hs yourself.

Loading calc.hs directly with :load calc succeeds on its own (as the Callout above shows for Wrong.hs) — but that does not help an import, which searches by module name, not by what has already been loaded.

questions.question: module MyCalculator (addTwo, averageTwo) where — with roundTo2 defined below but not listed. Can code that imports MyCalculator call roundTo2?
options: No — only addTwo and averageTwo are visible to importers; roundTo2 stays private to the module
Yes — every top-level definition is always visible to importers, regardless of the export list
Yes, but only if the importer uses a qualified import
No — none of the three functions are visible, because an export list hides everything by default
questions.explanation: An export list restricts what importers can see to exactly the names listed. addTwo and averageTwo are listed, so they are visible; roundTo2 is not listed, so it is private to the module and out of scope for any importer.
optionFeedback: Correct — the export list is exactly what makes roundTo2 invisible outside the module, while addTwo and averageTwo remain usable.
Without an export list, every definition would be exported by default — but this module has an explicit list, and it names only two of the three functions.
Qualifying an import changes how a name is written (Map.foo vs. foo), not which names are in scope in the first place; roundTo2 was never exported under either form.
The two listed names, addTwo and averageTwo, are exactly the ones an export list makes visible — only the unlisted roundTo2 is hidden.

questions.question: Why does exporting fewer names make a module easier to change later?
options: Because anything exported is something other code may come to depend on; keeping the rest private means you can rewrite it freely without breaking any caller
Because Haskell compiles modules with smaller export lists faster
Because a smaller export list means fewer functions need type signatures
It doesn't — export lists are purely a documentation convention with no real effect
questions.explanation: This is the practical meaning of 'loosely coupled' from earlier in this lesson: a caller can only depend on what it can see. Whatever stays unexported can be rewritten, renamed, or removed entirely without any importer's code breaking.
optionFeedback: Correct — the benefit is about safety when changing code later, not about anything to do with compilation speed.
Export lists have nothing to do with compile speed; the reasoning here is entirely about what callers can come to depend on.
Every function still needs its own type signature regardless of whether it appears in the export list; the two are unrelated.
The export list has a real enforcement effect — GHC actually removes unlisted names from what an importer can see, as the previous question's scenario shows.

deeper-reasoning-module-boundaries-and-f.title: Deeper reasoning: module boundaries and file names

questions.question: A student saves a file called Wrong.hs that begins with module MyCalculator where. Loading Wrong.hs in GHCi succeeds and the functions work, so the student concludes that file names do not matter. Later a second file that says import MyCalculator fails to load with a message that MyCalculator cannot be found. Which explanation accounts for both observations?
options: The first load should also have failed, so the success was a bug that has since been fixed.

Loading a single file directly does not require its name to match its module, so the first step succeeds. When another module imports MyCalculator, GHC looks for a file called MyCalculator.hs in its search path, and the module in Wrong.hs is not found under that name. The convention of one module per file, with the file named after the module, becomes a hard requirement the moment another module imports it, and the error appears in the importing file even though the module exists.
The import failed because module names are case-insensitive, so MyCalculator and mycalculator clash.
The import failed because a module can only be imported once per session, and Wrong.hs had already used the name.
questions.explanation: The mismatch is silent until a lookup by module name is needed. This is why the error is reported far from the cause, and why matching the names from the start saves time.
optionFeedback: GHC deliberately accepts a single file whose name differs from its module, so the first load is not a bug.
Correct. The cause and the symptom are in different files, which is what makes the problem confusing.
Module names are case-sensitive, and the mismatch here is between a file name and a module name, not a capitalisation clash.
A module can be imported by any number of other modules. The failure is about locating it.

questions.question: A teammate defines the module below and then writes a main file with import Temperature that calls both celsiusToFahrenheit 100 and freezingPoint. GHC accepts the first call and reports a variable not in scope for the second. The teammate asks whether the importer or the module is at fault. Which assessment is the most accurate?
options: The importer is at fault: import Temperature should always bring in every name defined in the file.
GHC is at fault, because freezingPoint is defined in the module and so it must be visible everywhere.

Neither is at fault. The export list (celsiusToFahrenheit) makes the module's interface only that one name, and freezingPoint is private. If importers need it, it must be added to the export list. Keeping the exported set small is deliberate: whatever is exported is something other code may come to depend on, so hiding the rest leaves the module free to change its internals without breaking callers.
The error appears because freezingPoint has the wrong type; a Double cannot be exported.
questions.explanation: An export list is a statement about the module's public interface. Names outside it are internal, and an importer that tries to use them gets a scope error, which is the intended behaviour.
optionFeedback: Without an export list a module exports everything, but this module has one, so only the listed name is imported.
Visibility in a module is controlled by the export list, not by whether a name is defined. GHC is following the declaration.
Correct. The error reflects a design decision rather than a mistake, and the repair depends on whether the name should be public.
Double values can be exported like any other. Visibility, not type, is the issue.

questions.question: A student argues: "Splitting a program into modules is only a way to make files shorter, and it changes nothing about how I test my code." Which reply best describes what modularity gives, and how a module can be tested?
options: The student is right: modules have no practical effect except for the length of each file.

Modules help because they group related definitions with a clear purpose, can be loosely coupled so they are reusable elsewhere, and make a program easier to manage. A module can also be checked on its own: load it in GHCi with :load, call its functions at the prompt, and confirm they work before any program uses it. A fault found there is in that module alone, which makes it far easier to locate.
Modules matter only because Haskell requires at least two of them in every program.
Modules make testing impossible, because their functions cannot be called outside the main module.
questions.explanation: The advantages of modules are about organisation, reuse and isolation. Isolated testing is the practical payoff: a module with a small interface can be exercised completely without the programs that depend on it.
optionFeedback: The benefits go beyond line counts: reuse, loose coupling and the ability to test a unit in isolation.
Correct. The three advantages and the testing workflow all come from the module being self-contained.
A program can consist of a single module, and in fact many small ones do. Modularity is optional, though useful.
Functions exported from a module can be called from any other module, and from the GHCi prompt after :load.
